message.content:
### Your Rights as a Tenant in Texas (as of 2026) Below is a concise, practical guide to the key protections and responsibilities that apply to residential tenants in Texas. These rights are derived from the Texas Property Code, local ordinances, and federal law (e.g., Fair Housing Act). While this overview covers the most common issues, you should consult a local attorney or tenant‑rights organization for advice tailored to your specific situation. | Area | What You’re Entitled To | How to Exercise It | Common Pitfalls | |------|------------------------|--------------------|-----------------| | **Security Deposit** | • Deposit may not exceed **one month’s rent** (or two if the lease is for a month‑to‑month tenancy).
• Landlord must return the deposit within **30 days** after you move out, minus any lawful deductions. | • Keep a copy of the lease and a receipt of the deposit.
• Request a written itemized statement of deductions. | • Landlords sometimes keep deposits longer than 30 days.
• Deductions for “normal wear and tear” are not allowed. | | **Habitability** | • Landlord must maintain the premises in a **safe, sanitary, and livable condition** (e.g., functioning plumbing, heating, electrical, pest control). | • Notify the landlord in writing (email or certified mail) of needed repairs.
• Keep a log of all communications. | • Landlords may ignore minor repairs; you may need to file a complaint with the local health department or take legal action. | | **Repair and Deduct / Rent Withholding** | • If the landlord fails to repair a major defect within a reasonable time, you may:
1. **Repair it yourself** and deduct the cost from rent (up to the amount of the repair).
2. **Withhold rent** until the repair is made (but only after giving written notice and a 10‑day cure period). | • Document the defect and the cost estimate.
• Send a written notice to the landlord.
• Keep receipts and proof of payment. | • Withholding rent can lead to eviction if not done properly.
• Repairs must be for major defects, not cosmetic issues. | | **Entry Rights** | • Landlord may enter only for:
1. **Emergency** (no notice).
2. **Repairs, inspections, or showing the unit** (at least **24 hours’ written notice**). | • Keep a copy of the notice.
• If the landlord enters without notice, you can refuse entry. | • Landlords sometimes use “showing” as an excuse to enter without proper notice. | | **Privacy** | • You have a right to privacy in your rented space. Landlord cannot monitor your activities or install surveillance without your consent. | • Report any unauthorized monitoring to the Texas Attorney General or local law enforcement. | • Some landlords may claim “security” to justify cameras; this is generally illegal. | | **Discrimination** | • Protected under the **Fair Housing Act** and Texas law: no discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex, national origin, disability, familial status, or source of income (e.g., public assistance). | • File a complaint with the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) or the Texas Commission on Human Rights. | • Discriminatory practices can include refusing to renew a lease or offering different terms. | | **Lease Termination** | • **Month‑to‑month**: Either party may terminate with **30 days’ written notice**.
• **Fixed‑term**: Landlord may terminate only for cause (e.g., non‑payment, violation of lease). | • Provide written notice and keep a copy.
• If you’re being evicted, you’ll receive a **Notice to Pay Rent or Quit** (10 days) or a **Notice to Vacate** (30 days). | • Landlords sometimes give less notice or use “no‑cause” termination in fixed‑term leases, which is illegal. | | **Eviction Process** | • Texas requires a **court order** for eviction. The landlord must serve a **Notice to Pay Rent or Quit** (10 days) or a **Notice to Vacate** (30 days).
• If you fail to comply, the landlord files an **eviction lawsuit** (forcible detainer). | • Respond promptly to notices.
• Attend the court hearing; you can present defenses (e.g., landlord’s failure to maintain habitability). | • “Self‑eviction” (moving out before the court order) can still lead to a judgment and a record of eviction. | | **Rent Increases** | • For month‑to‑month leases, the landlord may raise rent at the end of each lease term, but must give **30 days’ written notice**.
• For fixed‑term leases, rent is fixed unless the lease allows for increases. | • Review the lease for any rent‑increase clauses.
• Negotiate or seek a rent‑control ordinance if your city has one. | • Landlords sometimes raise rent without notice or exceed the amount allowed by local ordinances. | | **Utilities** | • The lease should specify which utilities you pay. If not, the landlord must provide a written statement of responsibility. | • Keep utility bills as proof of payment. | • Landlords may try to shift utility costs to tenants without clear lease language. | | **Insurance** | • Tenants are typically responsible for renter’s insurance covering personal property and liability. | • Obtain a policy; keep a copy for the landlord. | • Some landlords require proof of insurance before move‑in. | | **Local Ordinances** | • Many Texas cities (e.g., Austin, Dallas, Houston) have additional tenant protections such as rent‑control limits, eviction moratoria, or mandatory mediation. | • Check your city’s housing department website. | • Ignoring local ordinances can leave you vulnerable to unfair practices. | --- #### Quick Checklist for Tenants 1. **Read the Lease Carefully** – Look for clauses on rent, security deposit, maintenance, entry, and termination. 2. **Document Everything** – Photos, videos, written notices, and receipts. 3. **Know Your Notice Periods** – 30 days for month‑to‑month, 10 days for rent‑due notices. 4. **Respond Promptly** – If you receive a notice, reply in writing and keep copies. 5. **Seek Mediation** – Many cities offer free or low‑cost mediation before court. 6. **Know When to Call the Police** – If the landlord threatens violence or refuses to comply with legal obligations. 7. **Consult a Lawyer or Tenant‑Rights Group** – If you face eviction, discrimination, or major habitability issues. --- #### Resources | Resource | What It Offers | How to Access | |----------|----------------|---------------| | **Texas Attorney General – Consumer Protection Division** | Advice on tenant rights, dispute resolution, and filing complaints. | https://www.texasattorneygeneral.gov/consumer-protection | | **Texas Commission on Human Rights** | File discrimination complaints. | https://www.tchra.org/ | | **HUD – Fair Housing** | National fair housing resources. | https://www.hud.gov/ | | **Local Housing Authority** | City‑specific ordinances, rent‑control info, mediation services. | Search “[City] housing authority” | | **Legal Aid of North Texas / Texas Legal Services** | Free legal help for low‑income tenants. | https://www.legal-aid.org/ | --- ### Bottom Line As a Texas tenant, you have strong statutory protections against unfair eviction, discrimination, and unsafe living conditions. Keep a clear record of all interactions with your landlord, understand the notice periods, and know that you can legally withhold rent or repair and deduct if the landlord fails to maintain habitability. If you encounter problems, use the resources above to seek help—whether through mediation, a complaint, or legal action.
